parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State three of the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.

markscheme_points.text: molecules are in (constant) random motion; (all) collisions between molecules are (perfectly) elastic; no forces between molecules (except during collisions); volume of molecules is negligible (compared with volume of gas); collisions involving molecules are instantaneous;

hints: Hint 1: Picture what an ideal gas is meant to be - a huge number of tiny particles flying about. What would you need to assume about how they move and how much space they take up?
Hint 2: Think about what happens when two molecules hit each other or hit the wall. Is any kinetic energy lost, and do they pull or push on each other between hits?

Hint 3: Recall the full list: random motion, elastic collisions, no intermolecular forces except during collision, negligible molecular volume, collisions take negligible time. Pick any three to state clearly.
parts.proper_answer: Any three: molecules in constant random motion; all collisions between molecules and with walls are perfectly elastic; no forces between molecules except during collisions; volume of molecules negligible compared to volume of gas; duration of collisions negligible.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Ideal Means**
Think of kinetic theory as a simplified model. Real molecules have size and attract each other, but for an ideal gas you ignore those complications so the maths works. You are sitting beside the gas imagining tiny dots whizzing around.

Step 2: **Motion and Collisions**
First, there are very many molecules moving constantly and randomly in all directions with a range of speeds. Second, when they collide with each other and with the container walls, the collisions are perfectly elastic, so total kinetic energy is conserved and no energy is lost as heat or sound.

Step 3: **Size and Forces**
Third, pick one more idealisation. The volume of the molecules themselves is negligible compared to the volume of the container. There are no attractive or repulsive forces between molecules except during the instant of collision, and that collision time is negligible compared to time between collisions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain how molecular movement causes the pressure exerted by a gas.

markscheme_points.text: molecules collide with (walls of) container; momentum of molecule changes during collision (with walls); change in momentum is caused by force on molecule by wall; molecule experiences force from wall so molecule exerts force on wall; many molecules exerting force across the area of the wall leads to pressure (on the wall);

hints: Hint 1: Start with a single molecule hitting the wall and bouncing back. What happens to its velocity and therefore its momentum?
Hint 2: Link that change in momentum to a force. Which law connects rate of change of momentum to force, and what does Newton's third law say about the force back on the wall?
Hint 3: Scale up from one hit to millions of hits per second over the whole wall area to explain steady pressure.
parts.proper_answer: Molecules collide with walls of container and rebound, so momentum reverses. Change in momentum implies a force on molecule from wall, so by Newton's third law molecule exerts equal opposite force on wall. Many molecules over wall area give total force per unit area = pressure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **One Molecule Hits the Wall**
Imagine one molecule flying toward the wall with momentum $mv$ and bouncing back elastically with momentum $-mv$. Its momentum has changed by about $2mv$. It has not gone through the wall, so something must have pushed it.

Step 2: **Force Pair**
Rate of change of momentum equals force, so the wall exerted a force $F$ on the molecule to reverse it. By Newton's third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. That is the key step many students miss - pressure is the wall's view of the collision.

Step 3: **From Hits to Pressure**
Now think of $N$ molecules hitting all the time in random directions. Each hit gives a tiny impulse. Added together they give a steady average force $F$ on the wall. Divided by wall area $A$, $$p = \frac{F}{A}$$ which is the pressure you measure.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Fig. 4.1 shows the variation with thermodynamic temperature $T$ of the mean-square speeds $\langle c^2 \rangle$ for two gases X and Y.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

Fig. 4.2 shows the variation with $T$ of the product $pV$ for samples of the two gases, where $p$ is the pressure of the gas and $V$ is the volume of the gas.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2

State three conclusions about the gases and their samples that may be drawn from Fig. 4.1 and Fig. 4.2. The conclusions may be qualitative or quantitative. Use the space below for any working that you need.

markscheme_points.text: Any three bulleted points from:; both gases are ideal; Up to 2 points from:; mass of one molecule of gas X is 3.3 × 10^-27 kg; mass of one molecule of gas Y is 6.6 × 10^-27 kg; mass of one molecule of gas Y is double mass of one molecule of gas X; Up to 2 points from:; sample of X contains 0.27 mol / 1.6 × 10^23 molecules; sample of Y contains 0.81 mol / 4.9 × 10^23 molecules; sample of Y contains treble the amount of gas / number of molecules as sample of X; Up to 2 points from:; mass of gas X is 5.4 × 10^-4 kg; mass of gas Y is 3.2 × 10^-3 kg; mass of gas Y is six times mass of gas X;

hints: Hint 1: Look at the shape of both Fig. 4.1 and Fig. 4.2. Both are straight lines through the origin. What does proportionality to $T$ tell you about ideal gas behaviour?

Hint 2: Recall the two key equations: $pV = NkT$ for the Fig. 4.2 gradient, and $\frac{1}{3}Nm\langle c^2 \rangle = NkT$ which gives $\langle c^2 \rangle = 3kT/m$ for the Fig. 4.1 gradient. Which gradient gives $N$ and which gives $m$?

Hint 3: Pick values at $T = 400\text{ K}$ from each graph to find gradients, then calculate $m = 3k / \text{gradient}_1$ and $N = \text{gradient}_2/k$. Compare X and Y for mass, number of moles and total mass.
parts.proper_answer: Both gases are ideal since $\langle c^2 \rangle$ proportional to $T$ and $pV$ proportional to $T$. Mass of one X molecule $\approx 3.3 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, mass of one Y molecule $\approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, so Y molecule is twice as massive as X. Sample X $\approx 0.27\text{ mol}$, sample Y $\approx 0.81\text{ mol}$, so Y sample has 3 times number of molecules. Total mass of Y is about 6 times total mass of X.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot Ideal Behaviour**
Both Fig. 4.1 and Fig. 4.2 show straight lines through the origin. That means $\langle c^2 \rangle \propto T$ and $pV \propto T$. That is exactly what ideal gas theory predicts, so both X and Y behave as ideal gases.

Step 2: **Use Fig. 4.1 to Get Molecular Mass**
From kinetic theory, $$pV = \frac{1}{3}Nm\langle c^2 \rangle = NkT$$ so $$\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3kT}{m}$$ Gradient of $\langle c^2 \rangle$ against $T$ is $3k/m$. At $T = 400\text{ K}$, $\langle c^2 \rangle_X \approx 5.0 \times 10^6\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$ and $\langle c^2 \rangle_Y \approx 2.5 \times 10^6\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$. So gradients are about $1.25 \times 10^4$ and $0.625 \times 10^4\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-1}$. With $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J K}^{-1}$, $$m = \frac{3k}{\text{gradient}}$$ gives $m_X \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $m_Y \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. The Y molecule is twice the mass of the X molecule.

Step 3: **Use Fig. 4.2 to Get Amount of Gas**
For an ideal gas $$pV = nRT = NkT$$ so gradient of $pV$ against $T$ is $nR$. At $T = 400\text{ K}$, $pV_X \approx 0.90 \times 10^3\text{ J}$ and $pV_Y \approx 2.70 \times 10^3\text{ J}$. Gradients are $2.25\text{ J K}^{-1}$ and $6.75\text{ J K}^{-1}$. With $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $$n = \frac{\text{gradient}}{R}$$ gives $n_X \approx 0.27\text{ mol}$ ($1.6 \times 10^{23}$ molecules) and $n_Y \approx 0.81\text{ mol}$ ($4.9 \times 10^{23}$ molecules). Sample Y contains three times the number of molecules. Total mass $Nm$ gives $m_{total,X} \approx 5.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg}$ and $m_{total,Y} \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$, so Y sample mass is about six times X. Any three such conclusions earn credit.
